summary: This unit covers the hand tools of the electrical trade at Level 3: choosing the right tool for each task, using it safely and correctly, and looking after it. You will learn about insulated tools, screwdrivers and torque tools, pliers, cutters, strippers, crimpers, conduit and enclosure tools, and the tools for chasing and marking out. You will also learn to plan and control a tool kit, inspect tools, and supervise how others use them.

blocks.p: Hand tools are tools powered only by you: screwdrivers, pliers, cutters, strippers, crimpers, knives, hacksaws, hammers, chisels, spanners and the rest. Almost every connection in an electrical installation is made with one. A good termination depends on the right tool, in good condition, used the right way; a bad one, made with pliers on a screw or cutters used as strippers, can run hot for years before it fails.

This unit is for Level 3 trainees. You already use hand tools. Now you are expected to choose the best tool for each job, plan and control the kit for a team, inspect tools and reject faulty ones, and correct the way others use them.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the tools for a job
List the tasks, list the tools each one needs, and check the kit against the list before leaving for site.
Work dead
Make sure the circuit is isolated, locked off and proved dead before any hand tool touches a conductor.
Choose and check insulated tools
Recognise properly rated insulated tools, inspect them, and take damaged ones out of use.
Drive and tighten correctly
Match the screwdriver or key to the screw, and tighten terminals to the maker's torque.
Cut, strip and remove sheaths
Use cutters, strippers, sheath strippers and knives without damaging conductors or yourself.
Crimp and terminate
Fit ferrules, terminals and lugs with the matching tool and die, and check each crimp.
Work conduit and enclosures
Cut, ream, thread and bend conduit; punch holes and fit glands with the right tools.
Chase, fix and mark out
Use hammers, chisels, levels and chalk lines safely and accurately.
Control the kit
Issue, count and return tools; keep a register; make sure nothing is left inside equipment.
Maintain tools and supervise others
Clean, sharpen and replace tools; spot misuse and correct it by showing the right way.

ul: Tool shops sell both metric and inch tools. Conduit, boxes, breakers and accessories come from North American, British and European makers, so one kit may need slotted, Phillips, Pozidriv and square-drive screwdrivers, and metric and inch spanners and hex keys.
Most buildings are concrete block with rendered walls and concrete slabs, so hammers, chisels and masonry fixings matter more here than in timber-framed countries.
Heat, sweat, humidity and salt air rust tools quickly. Cleaning and oiling are part of the job, not an extra.
Supplies are **110 V and 220 V, 50 Hz**. 110 V is not a safe voltage: the rules about working dead apply to every circuit.

blocks.p: Read the sections in order, with your own tool kit beside you if you can. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will show you each tool and watch you use it.

sections.title: Planning the tools and controlling the kit

blocks.h: From the job to the tool list

blocks.p: A team leader does not find out on site that the lug crimper is back at the Centre. Start from the plan, list the tasks, then list the tools each task needs.

head: Task
Tools
rows: Safe isolation
Lock-off kit, padlocks, tags, two-pole voltage tester and proving unit
Removing cable sheath
Sheath stripper, cable knife
Cutting and stripping conductors
Side cutters, cable cutters for large sizes, adjustable or automatic strippers
Fitting ferrules and lugs
Ferrule crimper; lug crimper with the right dies; the ferrules and lugs themselves
Terminating
Insulated screwdrivers of the right types and sizes, hex keys, torque screwdriver
Glanding and enclosure work
Knockout punch set, gland spanners, pump pliers, files
Conduit work
Hacksaw and blades, pipe vice, reamer, bender, die stock, fish tape
Marking out and fixing
Tape, level, chalk line, pencil, hammers and chisels, detector

blocks.p: Check the kit against the list **before** leaving, and inspect each tool as you check it. Replace anything missing or faulty. This is also the moment to check that the torque screwdriver and any measuring devices are in date.

ul: A **shadow board** or foam-lined case has a shaped place for each tool, so a gap shows at once that a tool is out.
A **sign-out sheet** records who has which tool. On a team job, issue tools by name.
**Count the tools** before any board cover, trunking lid or ceiling is closed. A screwdriver left inside a board can fall across the busbars when the door is slammed months later.
Clear out **offcuts** of copper, stripped insulation and loose screws as well. A strand of copper across two terminals is a short circuit waiting for the power to come on.
At height, carry tools in a **belt or pouch**, never in pockets or on top of the ladder. Where people work below, tie tools to a lanyard.
At the end of the job: clean, check, count and return every tool, and report faults so they are fixed before the next job.

blocks.p: The Centre or company keeps a **register** of its tools, especially insulated tools, crimpers and torque tools: each tool's number, its checks, the dates, the results and what was done about faults. The register shows that each tool is inspected and fit for use, and lets you trace a problem: if a crimper is found to be faulty, the register and the job records show which jobs it was used on.

blocks.note: Tool control is a safety system, not a way of catching thieves. Brief your team so that they see the count as part of the job, in the same way as proving dead.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Before any hand tool touches a conductor or terminal, the circuit must be **isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead**. Insulated tools do not change this. They are a last line of defence if something has gone wrong, not a way of working live. A slip can still bridge two conductors with the bare tip and cause an arc flash, and damaged insulation can still pass a shock.

flow: Identify the circuit
Switch off and lock off with your own padlock
Tag: name, date, reason
Check the two-pole tester on a proving unit
Test between all conductors, and each to earth, at the point of work
Check the tester again on the proving unit
Only now use hand tools on the conductors

blocks.note: A **neon tester screwdriver** must never be used to prove a circuit dead. It relies on a tiny current through your body to light its lamp, so it can stay dark on a live circuit: in bright light, through insulating boots or gloves, with a failed lamp or a dirty contact. Use an approved two-pole voltage tester, proved before and after.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: What makes a tool an insulated tool

blocks.p: A soft plastic grip is for comfort. It is not electrical insulation. A real insulated tool is made and tested to a standard (IEC 60900) and carries:

ul: the **double-triangle** symbol;
a voltage rating, usually **1000 V** AC;
the maker's name and, usually, the standard and the year of manufacture.

blocks.p: The insulation is tough, bonded to the metal, and covers everything except the working tip. On screwdrivers it runs down the shaft, so that only the tip is bare. A long, slim insulated shaft lets you reach a terminal deep inside equipment without bare metal passing close to other parts. Insulated pliers and cutters have guards on the handles to stop your hand sliding forward onto the metal.

head: Look at
Reject the tool if you find
rows: Handle and shaft insulation
Cuts, cracks, splits, holes, burns, swelling, or insulation worn thin
Bond between insulation and metal
Insulation that is loose, has slid along the shaft or has pulled back from the tip
Markings
No double triangle or voltage rating, or marks so worn that the rating cannot be confirmed
Working end
A rounded, twisted or chipped screwdriver tip; chipped or notched cutter blades; jaws that do not meet
Cleanliness
Oil, paint, cement or metal dust on the insulation; clean it off, then inspect again

blocks.p: A damaged insulated tool is **never repaired**. Tape, glue, heat-shrink or paint have not been tested at the tool's rated voltage, and they hide the damage from the next user. Tag the tool, take it out of use, report it, record it in the register and replace it.

blocks.h: Other safety points for hand tools

ul: Wear **safety glasses** when cutting conductors, cable ties and conduit, and when chiselling. Cut ends fly.
Cut and strip **away from your body and hands**.
Keep tools sharp and in good condition: a blunt or worn tool needs more force, and force is what makes tools slip.
Use each tool only for what it was made for. A screwdriver is not a chisel, a lever or a punch; pliers are not a hammer or a spanner.

A **steel fish tape** conducts. Never push one into a conduit, box or board that holds live parts or cables; isolate first, or use a non-conductive (nylon or fibreglass) one where the risk cannot be removed.

**Strain injuries** build up slowly. For long runs of repeated work, such as stripping and terminating hundreds of conductors, choose tools that fit your hand, with good grips and spring-opening or ratchet action, keep your wrist straight, change tasks when you can and take short breaks.

sections.title: Screwdrivers, keys, spanners and torque tools

blocks.h: Matching the driver to the screw

head: Screw head
Driver
Notes
rows: Single straight slot
Flat (slotted) blade
The blade must fill the slot: nearly as wide as the screw head and a snug fit in thickness
Cross, plain
Phillips (PH0, PH1, PH2 ...)
Made to push the driver out (cam out) when over-tightened
Cross with four extra fine lines between the arms
Pozidriv (PZ1, PZ2 ...)
Grips better than Phillips; common on European breakers and accessories
Slot and cross combined
The combination tip the maker names, or the best-fitting PZ or flat tip
Common on breaker and terminal screws; check the maker's instructions
Square recess
Square (Robertson) drive
Common on North American devices and panels
Six-sided socket
Hex key (Allen key), metric or inch
Used on lugs and large terminals; use the exact size

blocks.p: A tip that fits exactly sits deep in the screw, turns it without slipping and lets you reach the right tightness. A poor fit slips, chews up the head and leaves the terminal loose, even though it felt tight in your hand. A **Phillips driver in a Pozidriv screw** (or the other way round) looks close enough but rides up and rounds the recess; a flat blade in a cross-head screw does the same more quickly. A damaged screw head also means the next person cannot check or re-tighten the terminal.

ul: Hold the driver in line with the screw and push as you turn.
Replace a driver whose tip is rounded, twisted or chipped. Do not grind an insulated screwdriver's tip.
Never strike a screwdriver with a hammer, or use it as a lever, punch or chisel: this breaks the tip, the handle and the insulation.
Use the right size of hex key, metric or inch. A nearly-right key rounds the socket, and a rounded lug screw may have to be drilled out.

blocks.p: Glands, locknuts, bushes and bolted lugs are tightened with a **spanner of the right size** or the maker's gland key. Pump (slip-joint) pliers with their adjustable jaw are useful for holding gland bodies and conduit fittings, but they mark the surface and can crush a plastic gland; long-nose pliers and screwdrivers knocked round with a hammer do not tighten a locknut properly at all. A loose locknut on a metal box can mean a poor earth connection through the fitting.

Makers give the tightness for each terminal as a **torque** in newton metres (N·m), or in pound-inches (lb-in) on North American equipment. Too loose, and the connection has a high resistance and overheats. Too tight, and the conductor is crushed, the thread strips or the device cracks. Neither can be judged reliably by hand.

ul: Set the torque screwdriver to the maker's figure in the right unit. To convert: **N·m = lb-in ÷ 8.85**. A terminal marked 20 lb-in needs 20 ÷ 8.85 = 2.3 N·m.
Fit the bit that matches the screw, hold the tool in line and turn smoothly.

A **click-type** or slipping torque screwdriver clicks or slips when the set torque is reached. Stop there. Turning on, or re-tightening by hand afterwards 'to be sure', takes the terminal past the figure.
Use a torque tool for tightening only.
A torque tool is a measuring device: it has a number, a check date and a place on the register. A tool with no check record, or one that has been dropped, is checked before it is trusted.
Where the maker advises it, large lug connections are checked again for tightness after a period in service, because conductors settle.

blocks.note: Much of the equipment in Jamaican panels is North American, with torque printed in lb-in on the breaker or inside the panel door. Read it before you start, and write the N·m figure on your plan.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Type
Use
Not for
rows: Combination (lineman's) pliers
Gripping, twisting and cutting conductors
Tightening screws or nuts; hammering
Long-nose (needle-nose) pliers
Reaching into small spaces; holding and positioning conductors; forming loops
Heavy gripping or levering: the tips bend
Round-nose pliers
Forming neat loops in solid conductors for screw terminals
Gripping flat work
Pump (slip-joint, water-pump) pliers
Gripping glands, bushes and conduit fittings with an adjustable jaw
Terminal screws; anything a spanner fits properly

ul: **Side cutters** (diagonal cutters) cut copper and aluminium conductors. Ordinary ones must not be used on steel wire, screws, nails or fish tape: the hard steel notches or chips the blades, and a notched blade crushes and tears instead of cutting. Use cutters rated for hard wire, or a hacksaw.

**Cable cutters** with curved shearing blades, hand or ratchet operated, cut large cables (for example 16 mm² and above) with a clean, round end that fits a lug. Chewing through a large cable in bites with small cutters, or sawing it with a knife, flattens and frays the end. Most cable cutters are for copper and aluminium only, not for steel wire armour.
Cut **square**. Hold or cover the waste end and point it away from people: a stiff offcut can fly several metres.

Cut **cable ties** flush, with a tie tool or flush cutters. A tail cut at an angle with side cutters is sharp enough to slice the hand of the next person who reaches in. A **cable tie gun** pulls each tie to the same tension and cuts the tail flush.

head: Tool
Best for
Use it safely and well
rows: Adjustable wire stripper (screw stop or sized notches)
Single cores of one size, stripped neatly
Set the stop, or choose the notch, to the conductor size every time. A notch that is too small cuts into the copper; one that is too big tears the insulation.
Automatic stripper
Many conductors, or mixed sizes, quickly
Check the first few ends. If it starts to crush or nick the copper, adjust it or take it out of use.
Sheath stripper (guarded or rotary blade)
Removing the outer sheath of a cable without touching the cores
Set the blade depth to the sheath thickness; try it on an offcut first.
Cable knife
Large or unusual cables where no stripper fits
The most dangerous choice: cut only through the sheath, along the cable and away from your body and hands, and keep it sharp.

blocks.p: A nick takes away copper, so that spot has less area, a higher resistance and runs hotter. It is also a weak point: a solid conductor bent at a nick snaps, often after it has been pushed into the box, where nobody sees it. On a stranded conductor, every strand cut off by the stripper makes the conductor smaller than its rated size. If you nick a conductor or lose strands, **cut off the damaged part and strip again**. Tape or solder does not put the copper back.
Stripping with side cutters ('biting and pulling'), with a knife drawn round the core, or with your teeth, nicks the copper almost every time.

Strip just enough for the terminal: use the **strip gauge** on the accessory if it has one. With the conductor fully in, the insulation should come right up to the terminal, with no bare copper showing outside it and no insulation trapped under the clamp.

flow: Measure how much sheath to remove, so the sheath still enters the box or gland
Score or slit the sheath only: just through it, never into the cores
Peel the sheath back and cut it off cleanly
Inspect every core for cuts before you go on

blocks.note: A blunt knife is more dangerous than a sharp one. It needs more force, and when it slips it goes further and faster. Keep the blade sharp, or fit a new one.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A crimp squeezes a metal barrel onto a conductor so hard that the two become one solid piece. Done with the right terminal and tool, it is strong, has a low resistance and stays that way. Done with pliers or the wrong die, it looks similar and fails later.

head: Fitting
Where it is used
Tool
rows: Ferrule (bootlace ferrule)
On the end of a **stranded or flexible** conductor going into a screw or clamp terminal, so that no strand strays and the clamp bears on solid metal
Ferrule crimper
Insulated terminal: ring, fork, pin, blade
Connecting small conductors to studs, screws and tabs in control panels and appliances
Ratchet crimper for insulated terminals
Cable lug (tube lug)
Bolting larger conductors, such as 16 mm² and above, to busbars, main switches and earth bars
Lug crimper (hand, ratchet or hydraulic) with the die that matches the lug

blocks.h: The usual colours of insulated terminals

head: Colour
Conductor size, about
rows: Red
0.5 to 1.5 mm² (about 22 to 16 AWG)
Blue
1.5 to 2.5 mm² (about 16 to 14 AWG)

blocks.p: Always check the size **marked on the terminal or the pack**. The colours above are the usual code for insulated terminals; **ferrule** colours follow different codes that vary between makers, so a ferrule is chosen by its marked size, never by colour alone.

flow: Choose the terminal for the conductor size and for the stud or terminal it goes on
Choose the tool and die made for that terminal
Strip to the length of the barrel, without losing strands
Push the conductor fully in, with no strands outside
Crimp in the right place; let the ratchet complete its full cycle
Look at it, then give it a firm pull

ul: A **ratchet crimper** will not open until it has closed fully, so every crimp gets the full pressure. A ratchet that releases early, or dies that are worn, mean under-pressed crimps: tag the tool and take it out of use.
On a lug, the die is marked with the size and usually leaves that mark on the barrel, so an inspector can see that the right die was used. Follow the maker on the number and order of crimps.

**Check by eye**: crimped in the right place, the right die mark, no cracks, no stray strands, the conductor visible at the inspection hole or the end of the barrel, the insulation close to the barrel.
**Check by pulling**: a good crimp does not move. Do not bend it back and forth, heat it or hammer it: those damage a good crimp and prove nothing.

blocks.note: Pliers, side cutters and a hammer and punch are not crimping tools. They dent the barrel instead of compressing it all round, and the joint has a fraction of the strength and many times the resistance.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Solid conductor under a screw head:** form a loop with round-nose or long-nose pliers and place it **clockwise**, the way the screw tightens, so that tightening draws the loop in instead of pushing it out.

**Stranded conductor in a pillar terminal:** where no ferrule is used and the maker allows it, twist the strands together neatly, so that none strays outside the terminal. Never cut strands off to make the conductor fit.
**Do not tin** (solder) the end of a stranded conductor that will go under a screw. Solder slowly flattens under pressure, and the terminal works loose.
One conductor per terminal unless the terminal is marked for more.

blocks.p: Push the conductor fully home, tighten with a driver that fits to the maker's torque, check that no bare copper shows and no insulation is under the clamp, then give the conductor a gentle pull. Dress the conductors neatly so that each can be traced and nothing is strained.

head: Conduit
Tool
Points
rows: PVC
Ratchet PVC conduit cutter, or a fine hacksaw
The cutter gives quick, square cuts with no swarf. Keep fingers clear of the blade. In very thick or cold-brittle conduit, use the saw.
Steel
Hacksaw with a fine blade, with the conduit held in a pipe vice
About 32 teeth per 25 mm for thin-walled conduit, about 24 for thicker walls. Cut square, using the full length of the blade.

ul: **Three teeth rule:** at least three teeth must be on the metal at once. With fewer, the teeth straddle the thin wall, snag and snap off. That is why thin walls need fine blades.
Fit the blade with its teeth pointing **away from the handle**, so that it cuts on the push stroke, and tension it firmly. Ease the pressure on the return stroke.
Hold conduit in a **pipe vice**: a bench or tripod vice with V-shaped jaws or a chain that grips round tube without flattening it. Flat vice jaws crush thin conduit or let it spin.

blocks.p: Every cut leaves a sharp **burr** on the inside edge. Drawn past it, cable insulation is sliced open, often where nobody will ever see it. Remove the burr from every cut end with a **conduit reamer** or a half-round or round file, and clean the outside edge too.

Where steel conduit is screwed into fittings, the thread is cut with a **die stock** (stocks and dies). Start square, use cutting compound, and turn back a part-turn every turn or so to break and clear the chips. If the die binds or the thread tears, stop: add compound, clear the chips and check that the die is sharp and clean. Ream again after threading, and clean off the swarf and oil.

Steel conduit is bent cold in a **bender** with a former of the right size; PVC is bent with a bending spring, or with heat for larger sizes, as the maker says. A bend that is flattened, kinked or wrinkled has a smaller bore: cables may jam or be damaged when drawn in. Cut it out and make it again. Keep the number of bends between draw-in points low, as the code or specification requires.

head: Tool
How it works
Good for
rows: Knockout punch (chassis punch)
A pilot hole is drilled, the draw bolt passes through it, and a cutter is pulled through the metal into a die by turning the bolt or by a hydraulic ram
Clean, round, exactly sized holes with almost no swarf: the best choice in a board that already holds equipment
Step drill or hole saw
Cuts the hole by drilling
Quick holes in empty enclosures; makes swarf that must all be cleaned out
Pre-formed knockouts
Rings pressed into the box, removed with a sharp tap and twisted off with pliers
Standard boxes; remove only the ones you need

blocks.p: Metal swarf inside a board can bridge live parts when the supply comes on. Whichever method you use, work on a **dead** board, shield the equipment below the hole, and clean out every particle afterwards. File any sharp edge and fit a bush or gland, so the cable does not bear on bare metal.

ul: A **fish tape** (draw tape) is pushed through the conduit, the cables are fixed to it, and they are pulled back through while a second person feeds them in.
If the tape will not pass a bend, do not force it: try from the other end or from a draw-in box, and check for a flattened bend or a blocked conduit.
Use only a pulling lubricant made for cables. Oil and grease attack insulation.
Never push a steel fish tape into a conduit, box or board where it could reach live parts.

Use
Check
rows: Spirit level
Setting boxes, trunking and conduit level and plumb
Read it, turn it end for end on the same surface and read again. If the bubble moves, the level is out: have it checked or replaced.
Chalk line
A string coated in coloured chalk, pulled tight and snapped against the wall to mark a long straight line
Keep it dry and filled with chalk
Plumb bob
A weight on a string that shows a true vertical
Let it stop swinging before you mark
Tape, pencil and scriber
Measuring and marking positions and cut lines
Mark clearly; measure from one datum

blocks.h: Before you cut into a wall

ul: Check the drawings and **scan the wall with a cable and pipe detector**. Cables usually run straight up, down or across from switches, outlets and boards, so look at what is on both sides of the wall.
Isolate the circuits in that wall if there is any doubt.
Mark the chase **straight up or straight across** from the box, never at an angle. Later, anyone drilling or nailing can guess where a vertical or horizontal run is; nobody can guess a diagonal.

Keep to the depth and width the plan allows. A chase that is too deep or too long weakens the wall, and you must never cut into columns, beams, lintels or reinforcing steel without the engineer's approval. If the plan gives no limit, ask your supervisor.
Tell the occupants, keep other people out of the room, and cover or move furniture.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Club hammer (lump hammer)
A short-handled hammer of about 1 kg or more, used to strike chisels
Bolster
A wide-bladed chisel for cutting the two clean edges of a chase
Plugging chisel
A narrow chisel for removing the material between the two edges, and for raking out joints
Cold chisel
A plain hardened chisel for cutting metal, and for concrete and hard render
Claw hammer
Driving and pulling nails and clips; not for striking hardened chisels

flow: Scan the wall and mark the chase
Put on eye protection, gloves and a dust mask; clear the area
Cut both edges with the bolster and club hammer
Remove the middle with the plugging chisel, to the allowed depth
Fix and protect the conduit or cable
Make good with mortar or filler, flush with the wall
Clean up the dust and rubble

ul: After much use, the struck end of a chisel spreads and cracks into a **mushroom head**. Pieces can break off and fly when it is struck. Take it out of use until the head has been ground back to a clean, slightly chamfered shape by someone trained to use the grinder.
Keep the cutting edge sharp. Hold the chisel with a hand guard if one is fitted, and watch the cutting edge, not the head.
Check that hammer heads are tight on their handles and that handles are not split.
Do not strike one hammer with another, or use a hardened hammer face on another hardened tool unless it is made for it: hardened steel can chip.
Chiselling throws chips several metres. Everyone in the room needs eye protection, not only the person chiselling.

blocks.note: Most Jamaican walls are hollow concrete block, rendered both sides. The face of a block is thin, so a deep chase breaks through into the hollow core. In new work the conduit is built into the wall as the blocks are laid; chasing is for alterations, and should be planned with the builder.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: In Jamaica's salt, humid air, a tool put away wet with sweat is rusty in a week. Wipe tools at the end of each day and keep a little light oil on the joints and bare steel. Do not leave the kit in the open back of a pick-up or in a closed van in the sun.

blocks.p: When you stop someone, say what you saw, explain what it causes, show the right method and watch them do it. People usually misuse a tool because the right one was not to hand, or because nobody showed them why it matters. Doing their work for them, or saying nothing and fixing it later, teaches nothing.

blocks.h: At the end of the job

blocks.p: Clean every tool, check it, count it back against the list or the shadow board, sign it back in and report any fault, so that it is fixed or replaced before the next job. Tools left loose in a van, or sorted 'later', are how faults and losses go unnoticed.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can list the tools a job needs from its plan and check a kit against the list.
I can explain why safe isolation comes before any hand tool is used, even an insulated one.
I can explain why a neon screwdriver cannot prove a circuit dead.
I can recognise a properly rated insulated tool, inspect it and say what to do with a damaged one.
I can match a screwdriver or key to a screw and say what a poor fit causes.
I can set and use a torque screwdriver and convert lb-in to N·m.
I can choose the right pliers and cutters for a task and cut safely.
I can strip conductors and remove sheaths without damage, and say what to do if a conductor is nicked.
I can choose a ferrule, terminal or lug and the tool and die for it, make a crimp and check it.
I can terminate solid and stranded conductors correctly in screw terminals.
I can cut, ream, thread and bend conduit with hand tools.
I can choose a method for making a hole in an enclosure and keep swarf out of the equipment.
I can mark out and cut a chase safely, and make good.
I can check a spirit level, a chisel head and a hammer before use.
I can set up tool control: shadow board, sign-out, tool count and register.
I can clean and maintain hand tools and decide when to replace them.
I can spot misuse of hand tools and correct it by showing the right way.

terms: Bolster
A wide-bladed chisel used with a club hammer to cut the edges of a chase.
Burr
The sharp edge left inside a cut conduit, removed by reaming.
Cable tie gun
A tool that tightens a cable tie to a set tension and cuts the tail flush.
Cam out
A driver riding up and out of a screw recess as it is turned.
Chalk line
A chalk-coated string snapped against a surface to mark a straight line.
Club hammer
A heavy, short-handled hammer for striking chisels; also called a lump hammer.
Die stock
The handle and dies used to cut a thread on steel conduit.
Double triangle
The symbol on hand tools made and tested as insulated tools.
Ferrule
A small metal tube crimped onto the end of a stranded conductor before it goes into a terminal.
Fish tape
A long flexible tape pushed through conduit to draw cables in.
Hex key
An L-shaped six-sided key for socket screws; also called an Allen key.
Knockout punch
A cutter pulled through sheet metal by a draw bolt to make a clean round hole.
Lug
A terminal crimped onto a larger conductor so it can be bolted to a bar or stud.
Mushroom head
The spread, cracked struck end of a worn chisel.
Pilot hole
A small hole drilled first, for a draw bolt or a larger drill to follow.
Pipe vice
A vice with V-jaws or a chain that holds round tube without crushing it.
Plugging chisel
A narrow chisel for removing material from a chase or joint.
Pump pliers
Pliers with a sliding adjustable joint; also called slip-joint or water-pump pliers.
Reamer
A tool turned inside a cut conduit end to remove the burr.
Shadow board
A board with the outline of each tool, so a missing tool shows at once.
Sheath stripper
A tool with a guarded blade that removes a cable's outer sheath without cutting the cores.
Torque
Turning force, measured in newton metres (N·m) or pound-inches (lb-in).

c1.title: A new board at a Papine bakery
c1.text: Level 3 trainee Damion Reid leads two trainees, Keisha and Leon, terminating a new distribution board at a bakery in Papine, St Andrew. The board is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead. The circuits use 2.5 mm² and 4 mm² stranded conductors. The breaker terminal screws are marked PZ2, and the maker's label gives 2.0 N·m for the breaker terminals and 40 lb-in for the main terminals. The team's torque screwdriver is marked in N·m. The box of ferrules holds several colours from two different makers.

c2.title: Steel conduit at a Frankfield clinic
c2.text: Trainee Tamika Lewis and two trainees are installing thin-walled 20 mm steel conduit along a corridor of a clinic in Frankfield, Clarendon. Their kit has a hacksaw with blades of 18, 24 and 32 teeth per 25 mm, a pipe vice, a flat-jawed bench vice, a conduit reamer, a die stock with cutting compound and a hand bender. One of the bends made that morning has come out flattened on the inside of the curve.

c3.title: A chase in a Cambridge house
c3.text: In an occupied concrete-block house in Cambridge, St James, trainee Odean Hamilton must cut a chase from a new outlet box to an existing conduit box 600 mm above it and a little to one side. He has a club hammer, a bolster, a plugging chisel, a cable and pipe detector, and a cold chisel whose struck end has spread and cracked. There is a light switch on the other side of the same wall.

c4.title: The monthly tool check in Seaforth
c4.text: At a training centre in Seaforth, St Thomas, instructor Mr Wendell Pryce and his Level 3 trainees are doing the monthly check of electrical tool kit 4. They find: insulated pliers with a 3 mm split in one handle's insulation; a ratchet crimper that opens before it has closed fully; a blunt cable knife; and a torque screwdriver with no number and no check record. A trainee offers to wrap the split handle in insulating tape.

c5.title: Second fix at a Toll Gate housing scheme
c5.text: Kevaughn Smith, a Level 3 trainee, supervises three Level 2 trainees doing second fix in new houses near Toll Gate, Clarendon. During one morning he sees Marlon knocking out and levering box knockouts with his insulated screwdriver; Kerry-Ann stripping 2.5 mm² conductors in the 1.5 mm² notch of her stripper because it 'grips better'; and copper offcuts and stripped insulation left lying inside the boxes and the board.

questions.q: The torque screwdriver reads in N·m. To about what figure should it be set for the main terminals?
o: 18 N·m
questions.why: N·m = lb-in ÷ 8.85, so 40 ÷ 8.85 = 4.5 N·m. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 354 N·m, which would destroy the terminal. Always check that a converted figure is sensible.

questions.q: Leon tightens the PZ2 breaker screws with a Phillips PH2 driver. What is the likely result?
o: The screws tighten faster, as PH2 is a sharper tip
Nothing: PH2 and PZ2 are two names for one tip
The driver rides up and rounds the screw recess
The driver locks into the screw and cannot be removed
questions.why: Phillips and Pozidriv look alike but have different shapes. A Phillips tip does not seat fully in a Pozidriv recess, so it cams out and damages it, leaving a terminal that feels tight but is not, and that nobody can tighten properly later.

questions.q: After the torque screwdriver clicks at 2.0 N·m, Keisha gives each screw an extra turn by hand 'to be sure'. Why must Damion stop her?
o: It can crush the conductor or strip the thread
It works the screw loose again after the tool's click
Hand tightening is only allowed on the neutral bar
The torque screwdriver must be used for the extra turn
questions.why: The maker's torque is the right tightness. Going beyond it can crush or cut the conductor, strip the thread or crack the breaker, and the terminals are then no longer at the figure the record says. When the tool clicks, stop.

questions.q: The ferrules are in several colours from two makers. How should Keisha choose ferrules for the 4 mm² conductors?
o: By the size marked on the ferrule or its pack
By colour: the same colour is always the same size
By trying each on the conductor until one is a loose fit
By taking the largest, so that any conductor will go in
questions.why: Ferrule colour codes differ between makers, so colour alone cannot be trusted. The marked size must match the conductor, and the ferrule is crimped with the ferrule crimper. A ferrule that is too big does not grip the strands.

questions.q: Which hacksaw blade suits the thin-walled steel conduit best?
o: 18 teeth per 25 mm, because coarse teeth cut fastest
24 teeth per 25 mm, fitted with the teeth facing the handle
Any of them, as long as the conduit is cut slowly
32 teeth per 25 mm, so three teeth stay on the wall
questions.why: On a thin wall, coarse teeth straddle the metal, snag and break. A fine blade keeps at least three teeth on the wall at once. The teeth should point away from the handle, so the saw cuts on the push stroke.

questions.q: Why should the conduit be held in the pipe vice and not in the flat-jawed bench vice?
o: Flat jaws magnetise steel conduit as it is cut
Flat jaws can crush the tube or let it turn
A pipe vice holds the conduit higher off the floor
A pipe vice cuts the thread as it grips
questions.why: A pipe vice has V-shaped jaws or a chain that grips round the tube. Flat jaws touch it on two lines only: tightened enough to stop it turning, they flatten a thin wall.

questions.q: While Tamika is threading a conduit end, the die begins to bind and tear the thread. What should she do?
o: Push harder and keep turning until the whole thread is cut
Finish the thread, then smooth the torn part with a flat file
Stop, add cutting compound and back off to clear chips
Heat the conduit end so that the steel is easier to cut
questions.why: Binding and tearing mean the chips are not clearing or the cut is dry. Cutting compound and backing the die off a part-turn every turn break and clear the chips. Forcing it ruins the thread and can chip the die.

questions.q: What should be done with the length of conduit whose bend is flattened?
o: Fit it, as cables are flexible and will pass a flat bend
Fit it, but pull the cables through it with more force
Hammer the bend back to a round shape and fit it
Cut the bend out and make it again with the bender
questions.why: A flattened bend has a smaller bore, so cables can jam or have their insulation scraped as they are drawn in, where the damage cannot be seen. Hammering does not restore the bore. The bend is remade with the right former.

questions.q: What should Odean do before he marks out the chase?
o: Tap along the wall and listen for hollow places
Scan the wall with the detector and check the drawings
Cut a small test hole at the centre of the planned chase
Ask the family whether the wall has given any trouble
questions.why: The switch on the other side shows that there is wiring in this wall. A detector and the drawings find hidden cables and pipes before the chisel does. A test hole is exactly how hidden cables get cut.

questions.q: The existing conduit box is above the new box and a little to one side. How should the chase run?
o: Straight up from the new box, then straight across
In one diagonal line, which is the shortest route
In a gentle curve, so that the conduit needs no bend
Across to the wall's corner, then up, then back again
questions.why: Hidden runs go straight up or straight across from accessories, where anyone drilling later would expect them. A diagonal or curved run cannot be guessed and is likely to be hit by a nail or drill.

questions.q: Which tool should Odean use to cut the two clean edges of the chase?
o: The plugging chisel and club hammer
The cold chisel, struck lightly
The bolster and club hammer
The club hammer on its own
questions.why: The bolster's wide blade cuts a straight, clean edge along each side of the chase. The narrow plugging chisel then removes the material between the edges. Without cut edges, the render breaks away raggedly.

questions.q: What should be done about the cold chisel with the spread, cracked head?
o: Use it, but strike it more gently than usual
Wrap the head in tape to hold the cracks together
Use it only with the lighter claw hammer
Take it out of use until the head is ground back
questions.why: Pieces of a mushroomed head can break off and fly into a face or an eye when it is struck. The chisel is tagged and kept out of use until the head has been dressed on a grinder by someone trained to do it.

questions.q: Why must Mr Pryce refuse the offer to tape the split pliers handle?
o: Tape makes the handle too thick to grip well in use
Tape is not tested to the tool's rated voltage
Tape is only allowed on the shafts of screwdrivers
Tape would hide the tool's number from the register
questions.why: An insulated tool's rating comes from insulation that was tested when it was made. Tape has had no such test and hides the damage from the next user. A damaged insulated tool is tagged, recorded, removed and replaced.

questions.q: What does the crimper that opens before it has closed fully mean for the kit?
o: It is worn in, so it will now crimp more quickly than before
It is fine for red terminals, but not for blue or yellow ones
Its crimps may be under-pressed, so it is tagged out
It needs a little oil on the dies before each crimp is made
questions.why: The ratchet exists to make sure every crimp gets full pressure. If it releases early, crimps can be made that look right but are weak and high in resistance. The tool is taken out of use until repaired, and recent work with it is checked.

questions.q: What is the right action for the blunt cable knife?
o: Sharpen it, or fit a new blade, before it is used
Keep it for trainees, as a blunt blade is safer
Use it with more pressure to get through the sheath
Use it only for cutting towards a bench top
questions.why: A blunt blade needs more force, so when it slips it travels further and faster, and it tears the sheath instead of cutting it. A sharp knife, used away from the body and only through the sheath, is the safer tool.

questions.q: What should happen to the torque screwdriver that has no number and no check record?
o: Use it, since torque tools never go out of adjustment
Have it checked and put on the register before use
Use it, but set it one mark higher to be safe
Keep it for undoing tight terminal screws
questions.why: A torque screwdriver is a measuring device. Without a check there is no proof that 2.0 on its scale is 2.0 N·m at the screw. It is checked, numbered and registered first. Torque tools are for tightening, never for undoing.

questions.q: Why must Kevaughn stop Marlon using his insulated screwdriver on the box knockouts?
o: Knockouts may only be removed after second fix
It makes the knockout holes larger than they should be
It damages the tip and the insulation of the tool
It magnetises the screwdriver, which attracts swarf
questions.why: Striking and levering break the tip and crack the insulation, so the screwdriver no longer fits screws properly and can no longer be trusted as an insulated tool. Knockouts are removed with a tool made for striking, then twisted off with pliers.

questions.q: What is the risk in the way Kerry-Ann is stripping the 2.5 mm² conductors?
o: The insulation will be left too long for the terminal
The stripper's blades will be blunted by the insulation
The conductor will be stretched to a longer length
The blades cut into the copper and weaken it
questions.why: A notch made for a smaller conductor closes onto the copper itself. The nick reduces the area, so the spot runs hotter, and the conductor can snap there when it is bent into the box. Damaged ends are cut off and stripped again in the right notch.

questions.q: Why must the copper offcuts be cleared out of the boxes and the board before the covers go on?
o: They add to the weight that the fixings must carry
An offcut can bridge terminals and cause a short
They make the insulation resistance read too high
Loose copper slowly corrodes the terminal screws
questions.why: A loose piece of copper can fall or be shaken across two terminals, or from a terminal to the earthed case, and cause a short circuit or an arc when the circuit is energised. Clearing offcuts is part of the tool and materials count.

questions.q: Which is the best way for Kevaughn to stop these habits coming back?
o: Redo the trainees' terminations himself each afternoon
Say nothing today and list the faults in his weekly report
Show the right method now and check their next few jobs
Take away the tools that were misused until next week
questions.why: A team leader corrects misuse on the spot: says what he saw, explains what it causes, shows the right way and then checks that it has stuck. Doing the work for them, or reporting it later, changes nothing on the job.
